sectionTitle: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Properties of waves

specStatements.text: Students should be able to describe wave motion in terms of their amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period.
The amplitude of a wave is the maximum displacement of a point on a wave away from its undisturbed position.
The wavelength of a wave is the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave.
The frequency of a wave is the number of waves passing a point each second.
period = (1)/(frequency)
period, T, in seconds, s
frequency, f, in hertz, Hz
The wave speed is the speed at which the energy is transferred (or the wave moves) through the medium.
All waves obey the wave equation:
wave speed = frequency × wavelength
[v = f λ]
wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s
frequency, f, in hertz, Hz
wavelength, λ, in metres, m
Students should be able to:
• identify amplitude and wavelength from given diagrams
• describe a method to measure the speed of sound waves in air
• describe a method to measure the speed of ripples on a water surface.
(Physics only) Students should be able to show how changes in velocity, frequency and wavelength, in transmission of sound waves from one medium to another, are inter-related.

Required practical activity 8: make observations to identify the suitability of apparatus to measure the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank and waves in a solid and take appropriate measurements.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 4.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

scopeNotes.statement: AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 4.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: AT 4 is an apparatus-and-techniques reference, not subject content, so it is honoured as a boundary rather than taught. All practical material written for this section stays inside the single technique AT 4 names for it — making observations of waves in fluids and solids, judging whether a piece of apparatus is suitable for measuring frequency, wavelength or speed, and taking those measurements. Nothing from another AT statement (electrical measurement, motion of objects, thermal or chemical apparatus) is introduced under this practical, and the AT code itself is never set as recall: no item asks what AT 4 is, or which AT skills a practical covers.

scopeNotes.statement: This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification names working scientifically and mathematical skills here as opportunities for development, listed elsewhere, not as content for this section. They are therefore exercised inside the wave material rather than taught as a separate syllabus: the mathematics used is only what these statements require — substituting into and rearranging T = 1/f and v = f λ, converting cm to m and kHz to Hz, and dividing a distance measured across ten wavelengths by ten. The working scientifically points raised are the ones the practical itself raises: repeating readings, measuring over many wavelengths or a long echo path to reduce the effect of uncertainty, and judging whether apparatus is precise enough for the quantity being measured. No WS or MS reference code is reproduced, taught or examined as recallable content.

concepts.definition: Any wave, transverse or longitudinal, is described using four quantities: amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period. Amplitude describes the size of the oscillation; wavelength describes how long one complete wave is; frequency and period describe its timing and are two ways of stating the same information, since T = 1/f. Wave speed is a further quantity, but it is calculated from frequency and wavelength rather than being one of the four descriptive quantities.

The amplitude of a wave is the maximum displacement of a point on a wave away from its undisturbed position. It is measured from the undisturbed line up to a crest, or from the undisturbed line down to a trough — never from a trough all the way up to a crest, which is twice the amplitude. Amplitude is a distance and is read on the displacement axis of a wave diagram.

The undisturbed position is where a point in the medium would sit if no wave were passing — its rest position. On a wave diagram it is the centre line about which the wave oscillates, and it is the line from which amplitude is measured. Displacement is measured from this line, so a point at the undisturbed position has zero displacement even though the wave is still passing.

The wavelength of a wave is the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave. Crest to the next crest, trough to the next trough, or any point to the matching point one wave later all give the same distance. Wavelength is given the symbol λ and measured in metres, m. A crest to the neighbouring trough is only half a wavelength.

The frequency of a wave is the number of waves passing a point each second. It is a counting rate — not a speed, and not a count of how many waves happen to be drawn on a diagram. Frequency is given the symbol f and measured in hertz, Hz, where 1 Hz means one complete wave passing each second.

The period of a wave is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point, and it is the reciprocal of the frequency: period = (1)/(frequency). A high frequency therefore means a short period. A wave of frequency 8 Hz has a period of 1/8 = 0.125 s, because eight waves share each second.

The specification states the relationship as period = (1)/(frequency), in symbols [T = 1/f]. Because the two quantities are reciprocals, the relationship rearranges to f = 1/T, so either can be found from the other. A period of 0.004 s gives f = 1/0.004 = 250 Hz. Period and frequency are never equal in value unless both are 1.

The specification gives period, T, in seconds, s. Period is a time, so its unit is the second — the same unit as any other time interval. Periods of waves are often small fractions of a second, so answers such as 0.004 s are normal and should not be rounded to zero or converted into hertz.

The specification gives frequency, f, in hertz, Hz. One hertz is one complete wave passing a point each second. Larger frequencies are often quoted in kilohertz, kHz, or megahertz, MHz: 1 kHz = 1000 Hz and 1 MHz = 1 000 000 Hz, so a frequency in kHz is multiplied by 1000 to convert it into hertz before it is used in the wave equation.

The wave speed is the speed at which the energy is transferred (or the wave moves) through the medium. It is not the speed of the particles of the medium, which only oscillate about their undisturbed positions and are not carried along with the wave. Wave speed is given the symbol v and measured in metres per second, m/s.

concepts.term: All waves obey the wave equation
concepts.definition: All waves obey the wave equation: it holds for transverse and longitudinal waves alike, and for waves in air, in fluids and in solids. Sound, ripples on water, waves on a string and electromagnetic waves are all covered by the same relationship, so a single equation links speed, frequency and wavelength for every wave met in this course.

The wave equation is wave speed = frequency × wavelength, in symbols [v = f λ]. It rearranges to f = v/λ and to λ = v/f. Because the speed is a product of the other two, a wave that keeps the same speed has a wavelength that falls as its frequency rises. Substituting f in Hz and λ in m always gives v in m/s.

The specification gives wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s; frequency, f, in hertz, Hz; and wavelength, λ, in metres, m. The equation only produces a speed in m/s if the wavelength is entered in metres and the frequency in hertz, so a wavelength quoted in centimetres or millimetres must be converted first, and a frequency in kilohertz must be multiplied by 1000.

concepts.term: Reading amplitude and wavelength from a diagram
concepts.definition: On a displacement–distance graph, amplitude is read vertically on the displacement axis, from the undisturbed centre line to a crest or trough, while wavelength is read horizontally on the distance axis, from one point to the equivalent point on the next wave. The two quantities are therefore measured on different axes, and confusing the axes is the commonest error when identifying them from a given diagram.

concepts.term: Measuring the speed of sound in air
concepts.definition: A workable method is to stand a measured distance from a large reflecting wall, clap, and time the echo returning; the sound has travelled twice the distance to the wall, so wave speed = (2 × distance) ÷ time. Distances of many tens of metres, and timings taken over several claps, are used so that human reaction time is small compared with the time being measured. An alternative method uses two microphones a measured distance apart connected to an electronic timer.

concepts.term: Measuring the speed of ripples on a water surface
concepts.definition: A ripple tank with a vibrating dipper produces ripples whose pattern is projected onto a screen below. The frequency is read from the signal generator driving the dipper, and the wavelength is measured with a ruler laid against the projected pattern, ideally across ten wavelengths which are then divided by ten. The wave speed is then found from v = f λ. A stroboscope or a video frame freezes the moving pattern so that it can be measured.

concepts.term: Sound passing from one medium to another
concepts.definition: When a sound wave crosses from one medium into another, its frequency is fixed by the vibrating source and does not change. The wave speed does change, because it depends on the medium — sound travels faster in water, and faster still in solids, than in air. Since v = f λ and f is fixed, the wavelength must change in the same proportion as the speed: a faster medium gives a longer wavelength.

In this practical, observations are made to identify the suitability of apparatus for measuring the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank and of waves in a solid, and appropriate measurements are taken. Typical judgements include using a ruler on the projected pattern rather than a stopwatch on a single ripple, reading the frequency from the signal generator, and measuring across ten wavelengths on a stretched string before dividing by ten.

misconceptions.question: On a wave diagram, which distance is the amplitude?
misconceptions.correct: The amplitude is the maximum displacement of a point away from its undisturbed position, measured from the centre line to a crest or to a trough.
misconceptions.misconception: The amplitude is the full height of the wave, from the bottom of a trough to the top of a crest.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The crest-to-trough distance is the most visually obvious measurement on a diagram, and everyday language calls that the height of a wave. The undisturbed line is often faint or missing, so students measure between the two features they can actually see.
misconceptions.correction: Find the undisturbed centre line first and measure from there. Crest to trough is twice the amplitude, so a wave whose crests are 3 cm above the line has an amplitude of 3 cm, not 6 cm.

misconceptions.question: How far is one wavelength on a wave diagram?
misconceptions.correct: One wavelength is the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave, such as crest to the next crest.
misconceptions.misconception: One wavelength is the distance from a crest to the trough immediately next to it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A crest and the next trough are neighbouring features, and the gap between them looks like one complete piece of the pattern. Students match adjacent features rather than equivalent ones.
misconceptions.correction: The two points must be equivalent, not merely adjacent: crest to crest, or trough to trough. Crest to the next trough is half a wavelength, so doubling it gives λ.

misconceptions.question: What does the frequency of a wave tell you?
misconceptions.correct: Frequency is the number of waves passing a point each second.
misconceptions.misconception: Frequency is how fast the wave travels through the medium.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech a high frequency sounds like something happening fast, and both quantities involve 'per second'. Students hear 'high frequency' and picture a wave racing along.
misconceptions.correction: Frequency counts waves per second at a fixed point; speed measures distance travelled per second. Two waves in the same medium travel at the same speed however different their frequencies are.

misconceptions.question: A diagram shows six complete waves. What is the frequency?
misconceptions.correct: The frequency cannot be read from the number of waves drawn; it is the number passing a point each second, which needs a time.
misconceptions.misconception: The frequency is six, because six waves are shown on the diagram.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are asked to count waves when finding a wavelength on a diagram, so counting becomes the default response, and a displacement–distance graph carries no time information at all.
misconceptions.correction: Check the horizontal axis. If it shows distance, the diagram gives wavelength, not frequency. Frequency needs waves counted against a clock, or a displacement–time graph.

misconceptions.question: A wave has a frequency of 8 Hz. What is its period?
misconceptions.correct: period = (1)/(frequency), so T = 1/8 = 0.125 s.
misconceptions.misconception: The period is 8 s, because the period and the frequency are the same number.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities describe the timing of the same wave and are often introduced in the same breath, so students treat them as interchangeable and simply carry the number across.
misconceptions.correction: They are reciprocals, not equals. A large frequency means a small period: eight waves each second means each one takes an eighth of a second.

misconceptions.question: In what unit is the period of a wave measured?
misconceptions.correct: The specification gives period, T, in seconds, s.
misconceptions.misconception: The period is measured in hertz, the same unit as frequency.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Period and frequency are linked by one equation and taught together, so the unit attaches itself to the wrong quantity. Hertz is the newer, more memorable unit and gets applied to both.
misconceptions.correction: Hertz counts events each second, so it belongs to frequency. Period is a length of time, so it is measured in seconds.

misconceptions.question: 400 waves pass a point in one second. How is this recorded?
misconceptions.correct: The frequency is 400 Hz — the specification gives frequency, f, in hertz, Hz.
misconceptions.misconception: It is recorded as 400 s, because the count was taken over one second.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The definition of frequency contains the word 'second', so students attach the second as the unit rather than recognising it as part of a rate.
misconceptions.correction: The second in the definition is the time over which the waves are counted, not the unit of the answer. A count each second is measured in hertz.

misconceptions.question: What is the wave speed?
misconceptions.correct: The wave speed is the speed at which the energy is transferred (or the wave moves) through the medium.
misconceptions.misconception: The wave speed is the speed at which the particles of the medium move up and down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams and animations show particles oscillating, and that is the visible motion. Students see moving particles and assume the wave is those particles travelling.
misconceptions.correction: The particles oscillate about fixed undisturbed positions and go nowhere overall; a floating cork bobs but is not carried to the shore. What travels is the energy, and its speed is the wave speed.

misconceptions.question: Which waves obey the wave equation?
misconceptions.correct: All waves obey the wave equation — transverse and longitudinal, in air, in fluids and in solids.
misconceptions.misconception: The wave equation only works for transverse waves such as water ripples, because those are the ones you can draw.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Wavelength and amplitude are first taught on a drawn transverse wave, so the equation feels tied to that picture. Longitudinal compressions look nothing like the diagram.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that all waves obey the wave equation. A longitudinal wave still has a wavelength — compression to the next compression — and a frequency, so v = f λ applies unchanged.

misconceptions.question: How are wave speed, frequency and wavelength related?
misconceptions.correct: wave speed = frequency × wavelength, that is [v = f λ].
misconceptions.misconception: The wave speed is the frequency divided by the wavelength.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that the three quantities are linked but not how. Speed formulas met earlier, such as speed = distance ÷ time, are divisions, so division is assumed here too.
misconceptions.correction: Check the units: Hz is 'per second' and λ is in metres, so multiplying gives metres per second. Dividing would give per-second-per-metre, which is not a speed.

misconceptions.question: Is the amplitude the same as the displacement?
misconceptions.correct: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the undisturbed position, not the displacement at any chosen instant.
misconceptions.misconception: The amplitude is simply how far the point is from the centre line at the moment you look at it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words are used loosely together, and on a diagram most points are somewhere between zero and maximum, so any of those distances looks like a candidate.
misconceptions.correction: Amplitude is one fixed value for the whole wave — the largest displacement reached. Displacement changes continuously as the point oscillates and is zero twice each cycle.

misconceptions.question: Which axis is amplitude read on?
misconceptions.correct: On a displacement–distance graph, amplitude is read vertically on the displacement axis and wavelength horizontally on the distance axis.
misconceptions.misconception: Both amplitude and wavelength are measured horizontally along the wave.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are distances measured in metres, so students treat them as the same kind of measurement and reach for the horizontal axis, which is where wavelength was first shown to them.
misconceptions.correction: The two quantities live on different axes. Amplitude is how far a point moves from rest, read up the displacement axis; wavelength is how long one wave is, read along the distance axis.

misconceptions.question: What unit does v = f λ give the answer in?
misconceptions.correct: With f in hertz and λ in metres, the wave speed comes out in metres per second, m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: The answer keeps the unit of one of the quantities used, so it is quoted in Hz or in m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students substitute numbers and copy a unit from the question rather than thinking about what the calculated quantity is. The equation has no obvious 'speed' symbol to prompt them.
misconceptions.correction: The unit follows the quantity being found. The specification gives wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s, and multiplying per-second by metres does produce metres per second.

misconceptions.question: A wave has a frequency of 2.5 kHz. What is this in hertz?
misconceptions.misconception: When converting kHz to Hz the student mishandles the factor of 1000 — dividing by it to get 0.0025 Hz, or using too small a factor such as 100 to get 250 Hz.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Unit conversions are remembered as 'move the decimal point by three' without a check on direction, and many conversions students meet do involve dividing.
misconceptions.correction: A kilohertz is bigger than a hertz, so there must be more hertz in the answer, not fewer. Multiply by 1000 when going from kHz to Hz.

misconceptions.question: Ripples have a wavelength of 40 cm and a frequency of 5 Hz. What is their speed?
misconceptions.correct: Convert first: 40 cm = 0.4 m, so v = 5 × 0.4 = 2 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: Substitute 40 straight into the equation to get 200 m/s.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number in the question is used exactly as printed, and centimetres feel like a perfectly ordinary unit of length, so no conversion seems necessary.
misconceptions.correction: The specification gives wavelength, λ, in metres, m. Any wavelength in cm or mm must be converted before substituting, or the speed comes out a hundred or a thousand times too large.

misconceptions.question: Can the speed of sound in air be found by timing a clap across the bench?
misconceptions.correct: No — over a short distance the travel time is far smaller than human reaction time, so a long path such as an echo from a distant wall is used instead.
misconceptions.misconception: A stopwatch and a metre rule are enough, because you can time the clap crossing the room.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Stopwatch-and-ruler is the standard recipe for speed in earlier work on moving objects, and sound is invisible, so students do not appreciate how quickly it crosses a room.
misconceptions.correction: Sound covers a classroom in about a hundredth of a second, while reaction time is about a fifth of a second. Use tens of metres, an echo, or electronic timing with two microphones.

misconceptions.question: How is the speed of ripples on water best measured?
misconceptions.correct: Measure the wavelength on the projected pattern and read the frequency from the dipper's signal generator, then use v = f λ.
misconceptions.misconception: Time one ripple with a stopwatch as it crosses a short gap and divide the distance by the time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Speed is first learned as distance divided by time, so students reach for a stopwatch. In a small tank the ripple crosses in a fraction of a second and is very hard to follow.
misconceptions.correction: A single ripple is faint, fast and hard to track. Freezing the pattern with a strobe or a video and measuring a wavelength, with the frequency read from the generator, is far more reliable.

misconceptions.question: A sound passes from air into water. What happens to its frequency?
misconceptions.correct: The frequency is set by the vibrating source and stays the same; the speed and the wavelength both change.
misconceptions.misconception: The frequency changes at the boundary while the wavelength stays the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know something must change when the medium changes, and frequency is the quantity they think of first because pitch is the property they can hear.
misconceptions.correction: The source keeps sending the same number of waves each second, so f is unchanged and the pitch does not alter. With v = f λ and f fixed, a change in v forces a change in λ.

misconceptions.question: A wave has a frequency of 8 Hz. What is its period?
misconceptions.misconception: The answer is 0.8 s, or 1.25 s, from mishandling the decimal point in the division.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reciprocals of small whole numbers are done mentally and the place value slips, especially when a calculator is not used and the digits 1, 2, 5 or 8 appear.
misconceptions.correction: Check the size of the answer: eight waves each second means each one lasts well under a second, so 0.125 s is sensible and 1.25 s cannot be right.

misconceptions.question: Does the amplitude appear in the wave equation?
misconceptions.correct: No. The wave equation is wave speed = frequency × wavelength; amplitude does not appear in it.
misconceptions.misconception: Wave speed is found from the amplitude and the frequency, because taller waves travel faster.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Big waves at sea look powerful and fast, and amplitude is linked to energy, so students connect amplitude to speed. The three wave quantities blur together.
misconceptions.correction: Speed depends on the medium, not on how tall the wave is. Only frequency and wavelength appear in v = f λ, and amplitude is measured on a different axis entirely.

misconceptions.question: How is [v = f λ] rearranged to find the wavelength?
misconceptions.correct: λ = v/f — divide the wave speed by the frequency.
misconceptions.misconception: Rearranging gives λ = v f, because the equation contains a multiplication.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see the multiplication sign in the original equation and keep it, changing which letters appear rather than changing the operation itself.
misconceptions.correction: To undo a multiplication you divide. Since v = f λ, dividing both sides by f gives λ = v/f, and a quick unit check confirms that m/s ÷ Hz gives metres.

misconceptions.question: What does the period of a wave measure?
misconceptions.correct: The period is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point.
misconceptions.misconception: The period is the number of waves that pass a point each second.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Period and frequency are the two timing quantities and are defined side by side, so the definitions get swapped. Both sentences mention waves passing a point.
misconceptions.correction: Period is a time, measured in seconds; frequency is a count each second, measured in hertz. Read the unit off the answer to check which one has been described.

misconceptions.question: Does sound slow down when it passes from air into water or steel?
misconceptions.correct: No — sound travels faster in liquids, and faster still in solids, than in air, so its wavelength gets longer.
misconceptions.misconception: Sound slows down in water and in solids because those materials are denser and harder to move through.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students borrow the idea from light, which does slow in denser media, and from everyday experience of things being harder to push through water.
misconceptions.correction: Sound needs particles to pass the vibration on, and closely packed particles do this faster: about 340 m/s in air, 1500 m/s in water and 5000 m/s in steel.

misconceptions.question: In the echo method, why is the distance to the wall doubled?
misconceptions.correct: The sound travels to the wall and back before the echo is heard, so the path is twice the measured distance.
misconceptions.misconception: The sound travels faster on the way back, so the outward and return journeys must be treated differently.
misconceptions.whyItArises: An echo sounds different from the original clap — quieter and later — so students imagine the reflected sound is a changed wave rather than the same wave returning.
misconceptions.correction: Reflection changes the direction of the sound, not its speed; the medium is still air. The timed interval covers two equal journeys, so the distance used is 2 × the distance to the wall.

misconceptions.question: Why measure across ten wavelengths and then divide by ten?
misconceptions.correct: Measuring a longer distance makes the uncertainty in each ruler reading a much smaller fraction of the result.
misconceptions.misconception: One wavelength is enough, and measuring ten is just the usual rule about repeating readings.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Repeating measurements is drilled as a general habit, so multiple-wavelength measurement is filed under 'repeats' rather than understood as a way of shrinking relative uncertainty.
misconceptions.correction: This is one measurement over a longer distance, not ten repeats. A 1 mm reading error on 20 mm is 5%; the same error on 200 mm is 0.5%.

misconceptions.question: What is an echo?
misconceptions.correct: An echo is the same sound wave reflected back from a surface, travelling at the same speed in the same air.
misconceptions.misconception: The wall makes a new, weaker wave that sets off more slowly than the original.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Echoes are quieter than the original sound, and students associate less energy with less speed, so the returning sound is imagined as a fresh, feebler wave.
misconceptions.correction: Only the amplitude is reduced by reflection; the speed depends on the medium and is unchanged, which is why the echo method works at all.

misconceptions.question: On a wave diagram, is the wavelength the distance from the centre line up to the top of a crest?
misconceptions.correct: No. That vertical distance is the amplitude. The wavelength is measured horizontally, from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the next wave, such as crest to crest.
misconceptions.misconception: The wavelength is the height of the wave — the distance from the centre line up to the top of a crest.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Amplitude and wavelength are introduced together as the two labelled lengths on the same diagram, and 'wave-length' sounds like a general measure of the wave's size, so students attach the name to the wave's most obvious dimension, its height.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the two measurements at right angles to each other: the amplitude is vertical, from the undisturbed centre line to a crest or a trough; the wavelength is horizontal, the repeat distance of the pattern, measured from crest to crest or from any point to the equivalent point on the next wave.

mcqs.stem: A transverse wave is drawn with its undisturbed position shown as a horizontal centre line. What is the amplitude of this wave?

options.text: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position
options.rationale: The specification definition: amplitude is measured from the undisturbed line to a crest or trough.

options.text: The vertical distance from the bottom of a trough up to the top of a crest
options.rationale: The most visible measurement on the diagram, but it is twice the amplitude.

options.text: The displacement of a point on the wave at the instant it is measured
options.rationale: Drops the word maximum; displacement changes continuously as the point oscillates.

options.text: The distance a point on the wave travels while one whole wave passes
options.rationale: Confuses the size of the oscillation with the path length covered in one period.

mcqs.stem: Which distance on a wave diagram is exactly one wavelength?

options.text: From the first crest drawn on the diagram to the very last crest drawn
options.rationale: Measures the whole wave train shown, not one repeat of the pattern.

options.text: From a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave
options.rationale: The specification definition; crest to the next crest is the usual example of it.

options.text: From the top of a crest to the bottom of the trough next to it
options.rationale: Adjacent features rather than equivalent ones; this gap is half a wavelength.

options.text: From the centre line up to the top of the crest above it
options.rationale: This is the amplitude, read on the displacement axis rather than along the wave.

mcqs.stem: What does the frequency of a wave tell you?

options.text: The speed at which a wave moves through the medium
options.rationale: A high frequency is heard as fast, but speed is distance per second, not waves per second.

options.text: The number of complete waves drawn on the diagram
options.rationale: Counting waves on a distance axis gives wavelength information, never a frequency.

options.text: The number of waves passing a point each second
options.rationale: The specification definition of frequency.

options.text: The time taken for one wave to pass a point
options.rationale: That is the period, the reciprocal quantity, measured in seconds rather than hertz.

mcqs.stem: Ripples pass a floating cork. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The frequency is the speed at which the ripples travel
options.rationale: That is the wave speed; frequency counts ripples passing each second.

options.text: The amplitude is the cork's displacement at any instant
options.rationale: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the undisturbed position.

options.text: The wavelength is the gap from a crest to the next trough
options.rationale: Crest to the next trough is half a wavelength; use crest to crest.

options.text: The period is the time one whole ripple takes to pass
options.rationale: The period is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point.

mcqs.stem: A wave has a frequency of 8 Hz. What is its period?

options.text: 8 s
options.rationale: Carries the frequency number straight across; the two quantities are reciprocals, not equals.
period = (1)/(frequency) = 1/8 = 0.125 s.
Decimal point misplaced; a period longer than a second cannot fit 8 waves into one.
Divides 8 by 10 instead of dividing 1 by 8.

mcqs.stem: A wave has a period of 0.004 s. Using [T = 1/f], what is its frequency?

options.text: 25 Hz
options.rationale: Comes from 1/0.04; the place value of the period has been read wrongly.

options.text: 4 Hz
options.rationale: Reads the digits of the period as the answer without taking the reciprocal.

options.text: 250 Hz

options.rationale: Treats period and frequency as the same number with a different unit.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the period of a wave is correct?

options.text: It is measured in hertz, the same unit as the frequency
options.rationale: Hertz counts events each second, so it belongs to frequency, not to a time.

options.text: It is measured in waves per second, like the frequency
options.rationale: Describes frequency; the period is a single time interval, not a rate.

options.text: It is measured in metres, like the wavelength
options.rationale: Confuses a time with a length; only wavelength and amplitude are distances.

options.text: It is measured in seconds, because it is a time
options.rationale: The specification gives period, T, in seconds, s.

mcqs.stem: In one second, 400 complete waves pass a point. How should this be recorded?

options.text: 400 Hz, because 400 waves pass each second
options.rationale: The specification gives frequency, f, in hertz, Hz, and 1 Hz is one wave each second.

options.text: 400 s, because the waves are counted over a second
options.rationale: Takes the second from the definition as the unit of the answer.

options.text: 0.0025 Hz, because frequency is one over 400
options.rationale: Takes a reciprocal that is not needed; 400 waves each second is already the frequency.

options.text: 400 m/s, because the waves move past the point
options.rationale: Attaches a speed unit to a count of waves each second.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the wave speed?

options.text: The speed at which particles of the medium move up and down
options.rationale: That is the visible oscillation; those particles are not carried along with the wave.

options.text: The number of complete waves that pass a point each second
options.rationale: This is the frequency, measured in hertz rather than metres per second.

options.text: The speed at which the energy is transferred through the medium
options.rationale: The specification defines wave speed as the speed at which the energy is transferred, or the wave moves, through the medium.

options.text: The speed at which the source producing the wave vibrates
options.rationale: The source sets the frequency; the medium sets how fast the wave travels.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the wave equation is correct?

options.text: It applies only to transverse waves, such as water ripples
options.rationale: Longitudinal waves also have a wavelength and a frequency, so the equation still holds.

options.text: It applies to light waves but not to sound waves
options.rationale: Sound obeys v = f λ exactly as light does; only the speed differs.

options.text: It applies only to waves whose speed stays constant
options.rationale: The equation holds in each medium separately, including where the speed changes at a boundary.

options.text: It applies to all waves, transverse and longitudinal
options.rationale: The specification states that all waves obey the wave equation.

mcqs.stem: How is the wave speed related to the frequency and the wavelength?

options.text: The wave speed is the frequency times the wavelength
options.rationale: wave speed = frequency × wavelength, the equation as the specification states it.

options.text: The wave speed is the frequency divided by the wavelength
options.rationale: Dividing per-second by metres does not give metres per second.

options.text: The wave speed is the frequency added to the wavelength
options.rationale: Quantities with different units cannot be added together.

options.text: The wave speed is the amplitude times the frequency
options.rationale: Amplitude does not appear in the wave equation at all.

mcqs.stem: The wave equation is [v = f λ]. Which rearrangement correctly gives the wavelength?

options.text: λ = f / v, the frequency divided by the wave speed
options.rationale: The division is the right operation but the wrong way round.

options.text: λ = v / f, the speed divided by the frequency
options.rationale: Dividing both sides of v = f λ by f gives λ = v/f.

options.text: λ = v f, the speed multiplied by the frequency
options.rationale: Keeps the multiplication instead of undoing it.

options.text: λ = v − f, subtracting the frequency from the speed
options.rationale: Subtraction of quantities with different units is not possible.

mcqs.stem: A student uses [v = f λ] with the frequency in hertz and the wavelength in metres. What unit does the calculated wave speed have?

options.text: Hertz, Hz, the unit taken from the frequency
options.rationale: Copies a unit from the question instead of identifying the quantity found.

options.text: Metres, m, the unit taken from the wavelength
options.rationale: Also copies an input unit; the answer is a speed, not a length.

options.text: Seconds, s, because speed always involves a time
options.rationale: Time appears in the unit, but only underneath: metres per second.

options.text: Metres per second, m/s, since the answer is a speed
options.rationale: The specification gives wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s.

mcqs.stem: A sound wave has a frequency of 2.5 kHz. What is this frequency in hertz?

options.rationale: Divides by 1000 instead of multiplying, making the frequency smaller.

options.text: 250 Hz
options.rationale: Multiplies by 100 rather than by 1000.

options.text: 25 Hz
options.rationale: Moves the decimal point one place instead of three.

mcqs.stem: Ripples on a tank have a wavelength of 40 cm and a frequency of 5 Hz. What is their wave speed?

options.rationale: Uses 40 cm as if it were 40 m, giving a speed a hundred times too large.

options.text: 2 m/s

options.rationale: Dividing frequency by wavelength (5 ÷ 0.4) gives 12.5; the wave equation is inverted.

options.text: 2 m
options.rationale: The right number, but a wave speed is quoted in metres per second.

mcqs.stem: A wave is shown on a graph of displacement against distance. How are the amplitude and the wavelength read from it?

options.text: Amplitude runs from a trough up to the crest above it
options.rationale: That distance is twice the amplitude; it must be measured from the centre line.

options.text: Both are measured along the horizontal distance axis
options.rationale: Amplitude is a displacement, so it is read on the vertical axis.

options.text: Amplitude is vertical, wavelength is horizontal
options.rationale: Amplitude is read up the displacement axis, wavelength along the distance axis.

options.text: Wavelength runs from one crest to the next trough
options.rationale: Adjacent but not equivalent points; that distance is half a wavelength.

mcqs.stem: A class measures the speed of sound in air. Which method gives the most reliable value?

options.text: Time the echo of a clap from a wall a measured distance away
options.rationale: A long path gives a time large enough for reaction time to matter little; speed = (2 × distance) ÷ time.

options.text: Measure how loud the clap is at two different distances
options.rationale: Loudness falls with distance but says nothing about how fast the sound travelled.

options.text: Use a stopwatch to time a clap crossing the laboratory
options.rationale: The sound crosses the room in about a hundredth of a second, far less than reaction time.

options.text: Ask two students to clap together and time the delay
options.rationale: There is no measured path length, and the delay is again dominated by reaction time.

mcqs.stem: In the echo method for the speed of sound, the distance to the wall is measured but twice that distance is used in the calculation. Why?

options.text: Because the sound must spread out in every direction from the clap
options.rationale: Spreading out reduces the loudness; it does not change the path length that was timed.

options.text: Because the wall creates a new wave that travels more slowly
options.rationale: Reflection changes direction and amplitude, not the speed of the sound in the air.

options.text: Because the sound travels to the wall and back before it is heard
options.rationale: The timed interval covers two equal journeys, so the path is 2 × the distance to the wall.

options.text: Because sound travels faster on its way back from the wall
options.rationale: The medium is unchanged, so both halves of the journey take the same time.

mcqs.stem: Which is a suitable method for measuring the speed of ripples on a water surface?

options.text: Count the ripples reaching the far edge and multiply by the depth
options.rationale: The depth of the water is not part of the wave equation.

options.text: Use the dipper frequency and a measured wavelength in v = f λ
options.rationale: Frequency is read from the signal generator and wavelength from the projected pattern.

options.text: Measure the height of the ripples and divide it by the frequency
options.rationale: Height is the amplitude, which does not appear in the wave equation.

options.text: Time one ripple with a stopwatch over a two centimetre gap
options.rationale: The ripple crosses that gap far too quickly to be timed by hand.

mcqs.stem: Why is a stroboscope or a video recording often used when ripples are studied in a ripple tank?

options.text: It increases the frequency of the ripples on the water surface
options.rationale: The dipper sets the frequency; a lamp or a camera cannot change it.

options.text: A stopwatch would time the ripples just as well
options.rationale: A stopwatch cannot reliably time fast ripples; freezing the pattern is why a strobe is used.

options.text: It makes the ripples taller so the amplitude can be measured
options.rationale: Amplitude is not needed here, and lighting does not alter the height of a ripple.

options.text: It freezes the pattern so wavelengths can be measured
options.rationale: A still pattern lets a ruler be laid across ten wavelengths on the projected image.

mcqs.stem: (Physics only) A sound wave passes from air into water, where it travels faster. What happens to its frequency and its wavelength?

options.text: The wavelength stays the same and the frequency increases
options.rationale: The source fixes the frequency; it cannot change at a boundary.

options.text: Both the frequency and the wavelength become larger
options.rationale: Only one of them can change, because the source sets the frequency.

options.text: The frequency stays the same and the wavelength becomes longer
options.rationale: With f fixed and v larger, v = f λ requires λ to increase in the same proportion.

options.text: The frequency stays the same and the wavelength gets shorter
options.rationale: Assumes the sound slows in water; in fact it speeds up, so λ grows.

mcqs.stem: (Physics only) Sound travels faster in a steel rail than in air. When a sound passes from the air into the steel, which quantity is fixed by the source and cannot change?

options.text: The frequency, which is set by the vibrating source
options.rationale: The source sends the same number of waves each second whatever medium receives them.

options.text: The wave speed, which depends on the source's energy
options.rationale: Wave speed is a property of the medium, not of the source.

options.text: The wavelength, because the wave keeps its shape
options.rationale: Wavelength must change when the speed changes, since f is fixed.

options.text: The period, which grows longer in the steel
options.rationale: Period is 1/f, so if the frequency is fixed the period is fixed too.

mcqs.stem: In required practical activity 8, which apparatus is most suitable for measuring the wavelength of ripples in a ripple tank?

options.text: A ruler measuring across just one ripple
options.rationale: Measuring across a single ripple is imprecise; ten wavelengths under the projected pattern are needed.

options.text: A ruler measuring the height of a single ripple crest
options.rationale: Measures the amplitude instead of the distance between crests.

options.text: A stopwatch timing one ripple crossing the tank
options.rationale: Timing gives a speed at best, and a very unreliable one.

options.text: A ruler placed under the projected ripple pattern
options.rationale: The projected pattern is still enough to measure across, ideally over ten wavelengths.

mcqs.stem: In required practical activity 8, waves are also sent along a stretched string. Why is the distance across ten wavelengths measured and then divided by ten?

options.text: The wavelength changes as the wave crosses the whole string
options.rationale: The wavelength is constant along a uniform string at a fixed frequency.

options.text: It reduces the effect of uncertainty in each reading
options.rationale: The same ruler uncertainty is a much smaller fraction of a ten-times-longer distance.

options.text: Measuring one wavelength alone would give the same result
options.rationale: One wavelength alone does not give the same accuracy; ten are averaged to cut uncertainty.

options.text: Ten readings must be taken in every school experiment
options.rationale: This is one measurement over a longer distance, not ten separate repeats.
